office.title: Indiana County Sheriff
office.summary: The sheriff is an elected county officer created by the Indiana Constitution who arrests offenders, keeps the peace, serves court papers, keeps order in county courts and runs the county jail [1, 2]. The Indiana Sheriffs' Association describes sheriffs as constitutional officers elected by the people, whose work includes operating jails, serving civil process, providing court security and coordinating emergency response [3]. Every county elects its sheriff in 2026 for a four-year term, and no one may serve as sheriff more than eight years in any twelve-year period [1].

facts.label: Term
facts.value: 4 years; the sheriff serves until a successor is elected and qualified [4, 1]

facts.label: Elected
facts.value: Countywide by the county's voters on the partisan general election ballot; all county sheriffs are elected in 2026 [1]

facts.label: Term limit
facts.value: No more than eight years in any period of twelve years (Indiana Constitution, Article 6, Section 2) [1]

facts.label: Qualifications
facts.value: Must have lived in the county for at least one year before the election, be registered to vote in the county by the filing deadline, and file a statement of economic interests; a sheriff who moves out of the county forfeits the office [1, 4]

facts.label: Pay
facts.value: A county may pay the sheriff a salary from the county general fund of at least 50% to 100% of the state minimum salary of a full-time prosecuting attorney, depending on county population [5]

duties: Arrests without a warrant people who commit an offense in the sheriff's view, brings them before a county court, and holds them while the arrest is investigated [2].
Suppresses breaches of the peace and pursues and jails felons [2].
Takes care of the county jail and the prisoners held there [2, 3].
Serves and carries out legal papers (process) directed to the sheriff by courts and the county commissioners [2].
Attends and keeps order in all courts of the county, which the Sheriffs' Association describes as providing court security [2, 3].
Takes photographs, fingerprints and other identification data from people held for crimes, and DNA samples for felonies [2].
Reports twice a year to the Indiana Department of Correction the average daily cost of holding a jail prisoner [2].
Holds state prisoners, including people convicted of Level 6 felonies, in the county jail, for which the state reimburses counties at a daily rate set in the state budget [7].
Coordinates emergency response and works with local police, prosecutors and community partners [3].

In a county whose council creates a sheriff's merit board by ordinance, appoints three of its five members, while the county police officers elect the other two; no more than two sheriff appointees and one elected member may belong to the same party [8].

Must report information to federal authorities when a person arrested for a felony or misdemeanor is believed to lack legal immigration status, and, since July 2026, notify the judge setting bail when holding a person subject to an immigration detainer [9, 10].
May supervise and inspect businesses such as pawnbrokers and secondhand dealers [2].

What the sheriff does not control: the county commissioners must establish and maintain the county jail building [11]; the county makes the appropriation for feeding prisoners and sets the sheriff's salary [5]; the prosecuting attorney decides which crimes to prosecute [12]; and judges decide bail [13].
recent_changes: February 2025: The Indiana Department of Correction said funding to reimburse county jails for holding Level 6 felons and state prisoners, then $40 per day, was exhausted for state fiscal year 2025; Tippecanoe County Sheriff Robert Goldsmith, then president of the Indiana Sheriffs' Association, called it very disappointing, and Rep. Greg Steuerwald (R-Avon) said everything owed would be paid [14].

2025: The new state budget raised the daily rate for Level 6 offenders to $42, raised the jail reimbursement line to $45 million and then $41 million a year, and moved to direct reimbursement with costs submitted within 60 days; Sheriffs' Association executive director Stephen Luce called the rate better than nothing, citing an association study that put the average cost at about $74 per inmate per day [7].
July 2025: The Department of Correction planned to begin paying about $12.7 million owed to county jails for housing state offenders [7].

July 2025: House Enrolled Act 1393 took effect, requiring jails to alert federal immigration authorities, with the county sheriff passing the information to federal officials, after felony or misdemeanor arrests when there is probable cause the person lacks legal status [9].

July 2026: Senate Bill 76 took effect, requiring sheriff's offices and police departments to notify the bail judge when they hold a person subject to an immigration detainer and barring local policies that restrict cooperation with federal officials; St. Joseph County Sheriff Bill Redman said his county already cooperates with ICE, while South Bend Mayor James Mueller said the city will protect the constitutional rights of everyone living there [10].

January 2026: The Sheriffs' Association's 2026 president, Porter County Sheriff Jeffrey Balon, listed jail overcrowding, staffing shortages, the drug epidemic and mental illness among the issues sheriffs raise with legislators [3].

November 2026: Public Question 1 asks voters whether courts may deny bail, for offenses other than murder or treason, when the state proves by clear and convincing evidence that no release conditions will reasonably protect others or the community [15]; Sen. Eric Koch (R-Bedford) said releasing some defendants before trial is too dangerous, while Zach Stock of the Indiana Public Defender Council raised concerns about jail overcrowding [13].

incumbent.name: Doug Vantlin
incumbent.party: Republican (party not confirmed in a source fetched for this profile)
incumbent.summary: Vantlin took office in 2019, according to candidate John Fuller [16], and is reaching the end of his permitted time in office, so he is not on the ballot [16]. His tenure included completion of a $36 million jail expansion [17].
record: 2019: Began his first term; candidate John Fuller said he was promoted to major when Vantlin took office [16].

February 2024: The $36 million Knox County Jail expansion, funded by a bond sale, a jail tax and remaining American Rescue Plan Act money, was nearing completion; it added holding cells, more padded rooms and a dedicated medical unit. Vantlin said, "We're crowded in the old part, and this is going to give us more room to work" [17].

October 2025: After the county council set two promoted officers' salaries at deputy rather than sergeant level while adopting the 2026 budget, Vantlin said the sheriff's merit board had approved the promotions in August 2025 and that the council's role is limited to funding positions; Council President Mike Morris said the council had not known of the merit board approval and could adjust pay by later ordinance [18].

August 2026: Vantlin said state law requires sheriffs to honor ICE detainer requests and that the jail holds detainees up to 48 hours; he said five detainees had been held in the county since Jan. 1 (two transferred to ICE, one released, two held on local charges) [19].
Candidate John Fuller, the office's chief deputy, put the office's annual budget at more than $8 million [20].

race_context: Open seat: Sheriff Doug Vantlin is reaching the end of his permitted time in office [16].
Five candidates filed: Republicans John Fuller, Michael Fisher, Paul Jones and Dan Short, and Democrat Brian Hagen [20].

May 5, 2026 Republican primary (unofficial): Dan Short 2,155 votes (40.55%), Michael Fisher 27.98%, John Fuller 18.01%, Paul Jones 13.46% [21]. Brian Hagen was unopposed in the Democratic primary with 998 votes [21].
Both nominees have law enforcement backgrounds: Short is a current Knox County deputy and retired military member; Hagen is a retired Vincennes police officer and former county coroner [20].
No general-election forums or debates were found in the sources reviewed.

candidates.summary: Hagen served with the Vincennes Police Department from 1984 to 2022 and was Knox County coroner from 2015 to 2020; he now works for Knox County Community Corrections [20].
background: Vincennes Police Department, 1984–2022 (described as a former captain); courthouse security officer, 2008–2010; elected Knox County coroner, 2015–2020 [20].
Full-time at Knox County Community Corrections since 2024, handling transport and processing of offenders [20].
Cites 39 years as a law enforcement officer and military service including an overseas deployment [16].
path_to_ballot: Unopposed in the May 5, 2026 Democratic primary, receiving 998 votes (unofficial) [21].

items: Plans to work with city police, university police, schools and the Vincennes Police Department [16].

on_incumbent: No statements by Hagen about Sheriff Vantlin's record were found. He has said the county needs an experienced, ethical sheriff [16].
plans: No detailed plan for the office was found beyond his stated intent to coordinate with other local agencies and schools [16].
endorsements_finance: Said in a Sun-Commercial candidate profile, "I am not asking for money; all I ask for is your vote as a registered voter in Knox County, Indiana" [20].
No endorsements or finance reports were found.
gaps: Coverage of Hagen is thin; no campaign website or post-primary interview was found.
Search snippets indicate Hagen ran for sheriff against Vantlin in 2018 and lost a 2020 coroner race; county results pages returned 404 and these were not verified.
No statements found on the jail, staffing, budget, drugs or immigration enforcement.

candidates.summary: Short is a Knox County deputy sheriff who joined the office in 2016 after 10 years with the Stockton, California, police, and is a retired member of the military [22]. He won a four-way Republican primary [21].
background: Joined the Knox County Sheriff's Office in 2016 after 10 years as a police officer in Stockton, California [22].

Lists sheriff's office roles as patrol road deputy, court deputy, jail officer, field training officer, community police officer, school resource officer, rifle team member, and SWAT logistics officer and operator [22].
Retired from the military after 21.5 years combined in the U.S. Marine Corps (infantryman, marksmanship instructor) and Army National Guard (military police), including a combat tour in Iraq [22].
Volunteers as a lieutenant with Knox County Emergency Management and with CERT [22].
path_to_ballot: Announced in July 2025 on his Facebook candidate page [22].
Won the May 5, 2026 Republican primary with 2,155 votes (40.55%) over Michael Fisher, John Fuller and Paul Jones (unofficial) [21].

items: Wants to expand community policing, including "coffee with a cop" events and more high-visibility patrols in towns and rural areas [20].
Would coordinate with mental health providers and allied agencies [20].
Said he is researching ways to address stray and abused animals [20].
Supports releasing body camera footage and giving the public timely information, saying "This isn't new, it is being done by agencies all over the country" [20, 16].

on_incumbent: No statements by Short about Sheriff Vantlin's record were found. After the primary he said he would work for everyone in the community regardless of party [23].
plans: Said he would start working as soon as he is sworn in [23].
endorsements_finance: No endorsements or campaign finance figures were found in the sources reviewed.
gaps: No campaign website found; his Facebook candidate page was not reviewed.
Sun-Commercial descriptions of his years in law enforcement vary slightly ("18th year" in July 2025; "19-year" officer in March 2026).
No statements found on the jail, budget, drugs or immigration enforcement.
A search snippet said Knox County has cooperated with ICE through a 287(g) agreement; not confirmed in any page read (the August 2026 Sun-Commercial article does not mention 287(g)).
